00.title: Your SAP-C03 architecture journey
00.imageBrief: Work from requirements to an architecture that can survive scrutiny across five exam domains.
learningNotes: Cloud architecture and AI integration: 25%
Security, compliance and governance: 25%
Cost optimization: 15%
Resilience, migration and continuity: 15%
Operational excellence and automation: 20%
00.decisionCue: A strong answer meets every stated constraint, including ownership, failure tolerance, cost and operational effort.

00.title: Read the constraints before choosing services
00.imageBrief: Separate facts from implied preferences before comparing services.
learningNotes: Underline hard constraints such as RTO, RPO, residency, latency and existing licenses.
Identify the traffic path, trust boundary, data lifecycle and who operates each component.
Eliminate choices that violate a hard constraint before optimizing cost or convenience.
When several options work, prefer the design with the fewest unnecessary moving parts.
00.decisionCue: The exam tests architectural judgment, not isolated product recall.

00.title: One workload, five architecture lenses
00.imageBrief: An international customer portal needs secure sign-in, regional data controls and a 30-minute recovery target.
learningNotes: Design: choose services around access patterns and latency.
Security: trace each identity and data boundary.
Cost: include replication, requests and inter-Region transfer.
Resilience: prove recovery with dependencies and a tested runbook.
Operations: make changes repeatable and observable.
00.decisionCue: A solution that satisfies four lenses but ignores a fifth remains incomplete.

00.title: How each visual lesson builds judgment
00.imageBrief: Learn the mechanism, compare neighboring choices, then test a realistic constraint change.
learningNotes: Trace the request and control plane in the diagram.
Explain why the nearest alternative fails in a concrete scenario.
Use a decision exercise to apply the idea under pressure.
Revisit mistakes after adjacent modules add new services or constraints.
00.decisionCue: The following identity module starts with authorization because every later architecture depends on it.

01.title: Identity decisions begin with the principal
01.imageBrief: A request succeeds only when the right principal can perform the right action on the right resource in the relevant context.
learningNotes: Name the human, application, AWS service or external machine that makes the call.
Identify which credentials that principal actually presents.
Locate the identity policy, resource policy and any guardrails that apply.
Check the requested action, resource ARN and condition values together.
01.decisionCue: A service diagram without identities cannot explain its security model.

01.title: IAM identities and credential lifetimes
01.imageBrief: Choose credentials according to where the caller runs and how long it needs access.
learningNotes: IAM roles provide temporary credentials to trusted principals and workloads.
IAM users may have long-term credentials and need stricter lifecycle controls.
An assumed-role session has its own session identity and expiration.
The account root user is for account-level tasks and should not run workloads.
01.decisionCue: Design a short-lived session path before considering a permanent access key.

01.title: The anatomy of a policy statement
01.imageBrief: Effect, Action, Resource and Condition jointly define a grant or denial.
learningNotes: Effect is Allow or Deny; an explicit Deny wins over applicable Allows.
Action matches API operations, while Resource scopes supported ARNs.
Condition checks request context such as tags, principal attributes or network origin.
Principal appears in resource-based and trust policies to identify who is covered.
01.decisionCue: Read the entire statement; a broad action can still be narrowed by a meaningful condition.

01.title: Allow, implicit deny and explicit deny
01.imageBrief: Start with default denial. A matching Allow can grant access only if no applicable explicit Deny blocks it.
learningNotes: No matching Allow produces an implicit deny.
A matching explicit Deny takes precedence across evaluated policies.
A guardrail can also withhold permission through its allowed maximum.
Do not treat a missing Allow as interchangeable with an explicit Deny in cross-account analysis.
01.decisionCue: Identify the exact statement or boundary responsible for the result.

01.title: Identity policies and resource policies
01.imageBrief: Identity policies attach to principals. Resource policies attach to supported resources and name a principal.
learningNotes: An identity policy expresses what its principal can request.
A resource policy can grant another principal access to a specific resource.
Within one account, an applicable Allow can come from either side, subject to evaluation rules.
Cross-account access commonly requires permission on the caller side and permission on the target side.
01.decisionCue: For cross-account questions, analyze both accounts and the kind of principal named by the resource policy.

01.title: Permissions boundaries limit delegated IAM
01.imageBrief: A boundary sets the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can receive through identity policies.
learningNotes: The identity policy must allow an action, and the boundary must permit it.
A boundary does not grant access by itself.
Use a boundary when teams may create roles but must stay within a central ceiling.
Resource policy grants to particular principal types have nuanced evaluation; check the named ARN.
01.decisionCue: A role creator cannot exceed a boundary merely by attaching an AdministratorAccess policy.

01.title: SCPs, RCPs and delegated permissions
01.imageBrief: Organization policies define account-level ceilings; they are separate from grants inside the account.
learningNotes: An SCP restricts the maximum permissions for principals in a member account.
An RCP restricts maximum permissions for resources in member accounts where supported.
Neither policy grants an action by itself.
Account-level design still requires IAM and resource policies to supply the actual Allow.
01.decisionCue: A permissive IAM policy cannot overcome a restrictive organization guardrail.

01.title: Session policies narrow a role session
01.imageBrief: A session policy passed to STS can reduce permissions for one assumed-role session.
learningNotes: The role identity policy remains the maximum starting point for the session.
The session policy intersects with that role permission set.
Use it to scope an otherwise shared role to a request, tenant or job.
A session policy never expands the role's effective permissions.
01.decisionCue: The same role can issue differently constrained sessions without creating a new permanent role each time.

01.title: Cross-account role assumption
01.imageBrief: Account A's caller assumes a role in Account B, then uses the resulting session to access B's resources.
learningNotes: A policy on A's caller permits sts:AssumeRole for the target role.
B's role trust policy accepts the caller principal and any required conditions.
STS issues credentials for B's role session after trust and authorization checks.
The role's permission policies and B's guardrails govern subsequent resource calls.
01.decisionCue: The trust policy controls who can become the role; the permissions policy controls what that role can do.

01.title: Trust policies and the confused deputy
01.imageBrief: A third-party service operates for many customers and needs a role in your account.
learningNotes: Trust only the provider principal that must assume the role.
Require a unique external ID agreed with that provider for the customer context.
Grant the role only the actions and resources the integration needs.
Confirm the provider supplies the correct external ID on every AssumeRole request.
01.decisionCue: An external ID helps prevent a provider from using one customer's role on another customer's behalf; it is not a password replacement.

01.title: Role chaining and session boundaries
01.imageBrief: When one assumed role assumes another, trace the session identity at every hop.
learningNotes: Each hop has a new trust-policy check.
Permission to call sts:AssumeRole must exist at the current hop.
Session duration and session policy restrictions can matter when roles are chained.
Avoid unnecessary chains that complicate attribution and expiration.
01.decisionCue: Follow the credentials actually used for the final request, not the human's original permissions.

01.title: ABAC with principal and resource tags
01.imageBrief: Attribute-based access control uses context instead of enumerating every resource ARN.
learningNotes: A policy can compare a principal tag such as Project with a matching resource tag.
Control who may set and change those tags; otherwise tags become a privilege-escalation path.
Use session tags when a federated identity supplies verified attributes.
Check whether the service and action support the condition keys you intend to use.
01.decisionCue: ABAC scales access patterns only when tag provenance is trustworthy.

01.title: Service roles and service-linked roles
01.imageBrief: AWS services may need a role to act in your account, but the role's purpose and lifecycle differ.
learningNotes: A service role is configured for a workload or service integration and has a trust relationship.
A service-linked role is associated with a specific AWS service and uses predefined service expectations.
Inspect what the service assumes and what resources it may change.
Do not replace a workload identity with an overly broad shared role.
01.decisionCue: Trace service-to-service access as a principal chain, just like human access.

01.title: IAM Identity Center for workforce access
01.imageBrief: Centralize workforce access to multiple AWS accounts and applications.
learningNotes: An external identity provider or the Identity Center directory supplies workforce users and groups.
Permission sets define access that Identity Center provisions into target accounts.
Assignments connect a user or group with a permission set and an account.
Users sign in through the portal or supported command-line flow to receive temporary access.
01.decisionCue: An account assignment and a permission set solve different parts of the authorization path.

01.title: SAML federation for workforce sign-in
01.imageBrief: A SAML identity provider asserts that a user authenticated and supplies attributes for the AWS access path.
learningNotes: The identity provider authenticates the person and issues a signed SAML assertion.
AWS validates the trusted provider relationship and maps the assertion to an authorized role or application.
Role sessions provide temporary AWS credentials when AWS API access is required.
Separate sign-in, provisioning and authorization; SAML authentication alone does not grant every account.
01.decisionCue: When the problem says workforce SSO across accounts, begin with Identity Center and the enterprise IdP.

01.title: SCIM provisioning is a lifecycle channel
01.imageBrief: SCIM synchronizes identities and groups; SAML handles authentication assertions.
learningNotes: Provision users and groups from the external directory into Identity Center with SCIM.
Disable or update identities centrally when employees move or leave.
Use SAML or another configured sign-in method to authenticate sessions.
Keep group assignments aligned with least-privilege permission sets.
01.decisionCue: A provisioned user still needs a sign-in path and an access assignment.

01.title: OIDC identity tokens and trust
01.imageBrief: An OIDC provider supplies signed tokens that AWS can validate for a configured federation flow.
learningNotes: Verify issuer, audience and subject claims against the role's trust conditions.
Use narrow subject claims to bind a workload or application to the intended role.
Exchange a valid token for temporary AWS credentials only when the workload needs AWS API access.
A token for the wrong audience should not be trusted for this role.
01.decisionCue: Issuer identity alone is insufficient; audience and subject commonly decide whether a token belongs to this workload.

01.title: Choose the federation entry point
01.imageBrief: Workforce users, application customers and external machines have different identity lifecycles.
learningNotes: Workforce access across accounts: IAM Identity Center with the enterprise directory.
Customer sign-in to an application: Cognito user pool or a compatible external application IdP.
AWS API calls on behalf of authenticated customers: Cognito identity pool where appropriate.
Servers outside AWS: IAM Roles Anywhere or supported OIDC federation based on the trust model.
01.decisionCue: The right federation product depends first on who the principal is.

01.title: Cognito user pools authenticate app users
01.imageBrief: A user pool provides an application user directory and issues tokens after sign-in.
learningNotes: Users authenticate through a native flow or a configured external provider.
The application validates tokens and uses claims to decide what its own APIs permit.
OAuth 2.0 authorization flows support delegated access patterns.
User-pool tokens are not themselves long-term IAM access keys.
01.decisionCue: Choose a user pool for application sign-in and token-based authorization at the app layer.

01.title: Cognito identity pools broker AWS access
01.imageBrief: An identity pool maps authenticated or supported guest identities to temporary IAM role credentials.
learningNotes: The application first obtains a supported identity token when authentication is required.
The identity pool selects an authorized IAM role and obtains temporary credentials.
The client can then call allowed AWS APIs directly under that role's policies.
Limit the role to the needed resources and account for untrusted client environments.
01.decisionCue: User pools answer who signed in; identity pools answer how an eligible client gets limited AWS credentials.

01.title: OAuth 2.0 roles in an application design
01.imageBrief: OAuth separates the client requesting delegated access from the resource server that enforces it.
learningNotes: An authorization server issues tokens for the intended audience and scopes.
The API checks token validity, audience, expiry and the requested scope.
An application role or fine-grained policy can further restrict tenant data access.
Do not mistake an OAuth scope for an IAM permission unless a deliberate bridge maps one to the other.
01.decisionCue: Application authorization and AWS IAM authorization operate at different boundaries.

01.title: The application authorization boundary
01.imageBrief: A customer token says tenant A, but the request asks for tenant B's report.
learningNotes: Authenticate the token and confirm its intended API audience.
Derive tenant identity from trusted claims or server-side mapping, not a client-supplied path alone.
Authorize the report against that tenant before reading the underlying S3 object or database row.
Use IAM to limit the API service's infrastructure access separately.
01.decisionCue: A valid sign-in does not imply permission to every application's data record.

01.title: EKS Pod Identity for AWS API calls
01.imageBrief: Associate a Kubernetes service account with an IAM role so a pod obtains scoped AWS credentials.
learningNotes: The pod uses the configured Pod Identity integration to obtain temporary credentials.
The role trust relationship allows the EKS Pod Identity service to assume it.
The role policy grants only the AWS APIs that workload needs.
Restrict access to node credentials; otherwise a pod may reach a broader node role.
01.decisionCue: Give each workload the role it needs instead of sharing a powerful node identity.

01.title: Workload identity on EC2, ECS and Lambda
01.imageBrief: Managed compute environments can supply temporary credentials through an attached role.
learningNotes: EC2 instance profiles expose an associated role to applications on the instance.
ECS task roles scope access to a task instead of the whole container instance.
A Lambda execution role governs the function's calls to AWS services.
Keep the trust policy aligned with the service and the permission policy aligned with the application.
01.decisionCue: Choose the narrowest workload identity boundary that the compute platform supports.

01.title: IAM Roles Anywhere for outside workloads
01.imageBrief: A server outside AWS can exchange X.509 credentials for temporary AWS role credentials.
learningNotes: A trust anchor establishes the certificate authority that AWS will trust.
A profile controls which IAM roles and session settings the workload can use.
The workload proves certificate possession and receives temporary credentials.
Plan certificate issuance, rotation and revocation as part of the architecture.
01.decisionCue: Roles Anywhere replaces static AWS keys for suitable external workloads but requires disciplined PKI operations.

01.title: Hybrid and multi-cloud identity trade-offs
01.imageBrief: Choose a bridge that your existing workload platform can authenticate reliably.
learningNotes: AWS-hosted workloads generally use their platform's managed IAM role integration.
External workloads with managed X.509 identity can use Roles Anywhere.
An external OIDC issuer can federate when claims and trust policies identify the workload precisely.
Avoid distributing static access keys to every server during a migration.
01.decisionCue: The trust root and credential rotation path matter more than a short initial setup.

01.title: Resource access across account boundaries
01.imageBrief: A central analytics account needs to read one bucket in a workload account.
learningNotes: Option A: assume a narrowly scoped role in the workload account and read as that session.
Option B: grant a specific external principal in the bucket policy, with caller-side authorization.
Account for KMS key permissions if the objects use a customer managed key.
Use organization IDs or other precise conditions where supported to avoid broad sharing.
01.decisionCue: Object access and KMS decryption are separate authorization decisions.

01.title: Data perimeters and trusted context
01.imageBrief: A data perimeter limits which identities, resources and network origins can interact with protected data.
learningNotes: Define trusted principals, resources and approved network paths explicitly.
Use appropriate organization and source condition keys in policies and guardrails.
Distinguish network location from identity: a private endpoint does not prove a caller is authorized.
Test expected service-to-service calls so controls do not break legitimate workloads.
01.decisionCue: A perimeter combines several controls; no single VPC setting creates it.

01.title: VPC endpoint policy: an additional authorization filter
01.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Constrain the endpoint path: A supported endpoint policy limits eligible principals, actions or resources for requests through that endpoint. It does not supply a network route, replace service authorization or govern requests that use another path. Evaluate applicable policies: The caller and resource must satisfy the relevant authorization rules. A same-account resource policy can sometimes supply the allow directly; do not assume every allowed request requires an identity-policy allow. Enforce the intended boundary: Use supported resource-policy conditions and network design when access must use a particular endpoint. Explicit denies and applicable SCPs/RCPs, boundaries and session policies still matter.
learningNotes: Constrain the endpoint path: A supported endpoint policy limits eligible principals, actions or resources for requests through that endpoint. It does not supply a network route, replace service authorization or govern requests that use another path.

Evaluate applicable policies: The caller and resource must satisfy the relevant authorization rules. A same-account resource policy can sometimes supply the allow directly; do not assume every allowed request requires an identity-policy allow.

Enforce the intended boundary: Use supported resource-policy conditions and network design when access must use a particular endpoint. Explicit denies and applicable SCPs/RCPs, boundaries and session policies still matter.
01.decisionCue: Endpoint reachability, endpoint filtering and service authorization are different checks.

01.title: IAM Access Analyzer and external sharing
01.imageBrief: Analyze resource policies for access beyond the account or organization you define as trusted.
learningNotes: External access findings reveal public or cross-boundary grants on supported resources.
Unused access analysis helps identify roles or permissions to reduce.
Policy validation and custom checks can catch problems before deployment.
Review findings in context; an intended partner share still needs ownership and evidence.
01.decisionCue: Use analysis before and after a resource-policy change, rather than relying only on manual inspection.

01.title: AWS Verified Access for application entry
01.imageBrief: Verified Access evaluates application requests using identity and device context under configured policies.
learningNotes: Integrate an identity provider and, when appropriate, a device trust provider.
Write access policies for the private application rather than granting all users network-wide entry.
Verify application endpoint placement, DNS and traffic path separately.
Use it for application access decisions, not as a substitute for the app's own record-level authorization.
01.decisionCue: Identity-aware access to an app and IAM permission to AWS APIs solve distinct problems.

01.title: Policy conditions that alter the answer
01.imageBrief: The exam often turns on a condition rather than a named service.
learningNotes: aws:PrincipalOrgID can restrict a supported policy to principals in an organization.
aws:SourceVpce can bind a request to a particular VPC endpoint where supported.
aws:PrincipalTag can express verified role or session attributes.
Check whether the service inserts context keys into the request and how service calls propagate them.
01.decisionCue: A condition key has value only when it is present and evaluated as intended for that request path.

01.title: Least privilege as a repeatable process
01.imageBrief: Define a narrow initial role, observe actual use, and remove unnecessary permissions.
learningNotes: Separate job functions and workload identities before writing policy JSON.
Scope actions and resources using service authorization details.
Apply conditions only when their behavior has been verified.
Review Access Analyzer and activity evidence; validate changes in a safe environment.
01.decisionCue: Least privilege requires ongoing evidence, especially when services and workload behavior change.

01.title: Troubleshooting AccessDenied systematically
01.imageBrief: The visible error is the end of a policy evaluation path, not the diagnosis.
learningNotes: Confirm the active principal with STS identity and the exact action and resource.
Check explicit denies, then identity or resource Allows, boundaries, session policies and organization guardrails.
Check role trust separately if AssumeRole fails before the final API call.
Inspect endpoint policies, KMS key policies and condition context when the path includes them.
01.decisionCue: Changing an IAM identity policy will not repair a missing role trust or a blocked endpoint policy.

01.title: Scenario: vendor access to customer data
01.imageBrief: A SaaS vendor processes data for 200 customer accounts and must read a bucket in each account.
learningNotes: Create a customer-owned role with the minimum bucket permissions.
Trust the vendor's designated AWS principal and require a customer-specific external ID.
Keep the external ID associated with the correct customer account in the vendor control plane.
Audit role sessions and review the trust relationship as the integration changes.
01.decisionCue: The external ID addresses the confused-deputy risk in a shared third-party service.

01.title: Scenario: workforce access to 80 accounts
01.imageBrief: An enterprise IdP owns employee identity; teams need different access in development and production.
learningNotes: Integrate the external IdP with IAM Identity Center for workforce sign-in.
Provision users and groups with SCIM where supported.
Create distinct permission sets for developer and production duties.
Assign groups to account and permission-set combinations; review access when group membership changes.
01.decisionCue: A single login experience does not imply identical privileges across accounts.

01.title: Scenario: consumer app with direct S3 uploads
01.imageBrief: Mobile users must upload their own objects without exposing a server-side AWS access key.
learningNotes: Authenticate users with a user pool or another trusted application IdP.
Use an identity pool for limited temporary AWS credentials if direct AWS API access is required.
Constrain uploads to the caller's permitted object prefix and validate the mapping.
Consider pre-signed URLs when the backend should mediate each upload instead.
01.decisionCue: Pick the access path based on whether the client truly needs AWS credentials.

01.title: Scenario: external batch servers
01.imageBrief: On-premises batch workers need to write to S3 while long-term access keys are prohibited.
learningNotes: Use IAM Roles Anywhere when workers have managed X.509 identities and can operate the required PKI.
Create a trust anchor and role profile that limits which role each workload can obtain.
Grant the role only the relevant S3 write actions and prefixes.
Design certificate rotation, revocation and logging before rollout.
01.decisionCue: Temporary credentials solve the AWS key problem; certificate governance remains an operational responsibility.

01.title: Scenario: a pod reads a single secret
01.imageBrief: One EKS workload needs Secrets Manager access; neighboring pods must not inherit it.
learningNotes: Bind the workload's Kubernetes service account to a dedicated Pod Identity association.
Grant its IAM role read access to the one secret and required KMS decrypt permission if applicable.
Keep other service accounts separate and restrict node credential exposure.
Test the pod's actual credentials and a neighboring pod's denied request.
01.decisionCue: The pod, rather than the node or cluster, should be the access boundary.

01.title: Scenario: stop unintended external access
01.imageBrief: A storage policy change could expose a regulated dataset outside the organization.
learningNotes: Use an external access analyzer to detect policy grants beyond the chosen zone of trust.
Add tested organization or principal restrictions to the resource policy as appropriate.
Use VPC endpoint policy and approved path conditions for requests expected from private workloads.
Validate legitimate service principals and partner exceptions before enforcing a broad deny.
01.decisionCue: Combine finding review with tested guardrails; an analyzer finding alone does not block a request.

01.title: Decision drill: which identity service?
01.imageBrief: Match the caller to the credential path before looking at the application architecture.
learningNotes: Employees using many AWS accounts: IAM Identity Center with assignments.
Customer signs in to a web application: Cognito user pool or an application IdP.
Authenticated mobile user needs constrained direct AWS API calls: identity pool.
External server with a managed certificate: IAM Roles Anywhere.
01.decisionCue: The distinction among user authentication, application authorization and AWS credentials is exam critical.

01.title: Decision drill: where did the Allow fail?
01.imageBrief: A role has an S3 Allow, yet PutObject fails. Investigate the complete request path.
learningNotes: Is the final caller actually that role session?
Does the policy match the precise object ARN and action?
Does an SCP, boundary, session policy, endpoint policy or bucket policy block the call?
Does encryption invoke a separate KMS permission check?
01.decisionCue: The nearest policy document is not necessarily the policy that decided the request.

01.title: Resource policy principal precision
01.imageBrief: A grant to a role ARN and a grant directly to a role session ARN can behave differently with implicit denies.
learningNotes: Inspect the Principal value in the resource policy before applying a simplified policy-intersection rule.
A direct grant to a role session principal can bypass an implicit deny in its identity policy or session policy within the same account.
An applicable explicit Deny still overrides the grant.
Prefer the intended role and resource boundary; test policy behavior when a design depends on this exception.
01.decisionCue: Policy evaluation has principal-specific exceptions. Never infer a final decision from one policy in isolation.

01.title: Identity architecture: final synthesis
01.imageBrief: Identity design is a chain of authentication, temporary credentials, authorization and evidence.
learningNotes: Workforce: IdP, provisioning, Identity Center, permission set and account assignment.
Application: user token, API authorization and optional scoped AWS credentials.
Workload: platform role, OIDC or X.509 federation with short-lived sessions.
Governance: policy ceilings, data perimeter and Access Analyzer review.
01.decisionCue: For any exam scenario, draw the caller and every trust boundary before choosing a service.

01.title: Directory identity: AD DS and AD FS do different jobs
01.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Directory objects: Active Directory Domain Services stores users, computers, groups and other domain objects. Domain controllers serve the domain; trees and forests define directory structure and trust boundaries. Federation across applications: AD FS is a federation service that can authenticate a corporate user and issue a SAML assertion for application sign-in. An assertion is not an AWS access key. AWS access follows trust: For AWS federation, configure the identity-provider and role trust, then obtain the intended AWS session. Directory trust, SAML federation and AWS permission policies are separate controls.

01.title: Choose Managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector or Simple AD
01.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Managed Microsoft AD: A managed Microsoft directory in AWS supports traditional AD-aware workloads and supported trusts/integrations. AWS operates domain controllers; you still manage users, groups and application permissions. AD Connector: A gateway forwards supported directory requests to an existing AD. Users remain in that directory; connectivity and directory availability matter. It is not a replica or an offline credential cache. 01.title: Managed Microsoft AD: availability, sharing and integrations
01.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Operate across AZs: Managed domain controllers are deployed across two AZs; supported scaling and backups protect directory operations. Directory resilience does not automatically make each dependent application resilient. Connect compatible workloads: Windows domain join, supported RDS SQL Server, virtual desktops and traditional AD applications require the right directory, DNS and network paths. 01.title: Trust and replication preserve different directory boundaries
01.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Trust is not synchronization: One-way or two-way supported external/forest trusts allow authentication across directory boundaries. Trust direction defines which domain's users can access the other domain's resources; it does not copy every user. Prepare the hybrid path: DX/VPN routing, DNS forwarding, required ports and compatible directory configuration must work before a trust can be used. Verify both authentication and application authorization. Replicate where required: A self-managed domain-controller replica on EC2 can keep that existing domain closer to workloads. 01.title: STS APIs create different kinds of temporary sessions
01.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Assume a role: AssumeRole creates a role session within an account or across accounts. User and broker sessions: GetSessionToken supplies an eligible IAM user's temporary credentials, including supported MFA context. 01.title: Policy conditions: choose the operator and context key
01.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Match the value's type: StringEquals/StringLike, numeric, date, Bool, IP-address and ARN operators solve different comparisons. Use variables deliberately: Supported variables can scope a resource or condition to context such as a principal tag or username. A variable that fits an IAM user may not exist for an assumed-role session. Test missing context: Null checks key presence; IfExists and negated operators alter missing-key behavior. Test both an expected request and a request without the key before using the condition as a security boundary.

01.title: Managed policies: broad access is not an explicit deny
01.imageBrief: Module 09 style. AdministratorAccess: A broad identity-policy allow still operates inside applicable organization guardrails, resource controls and explicit denies. AdministratorAccess does not bypass every authorization boundary. PowerUserAccess: This AWS-managed policy allows broad service use while excluding broad identity/account administration, with specific exceptions defined by its current version. Inspect the live policy rather than memorizing a frozen exception list. 02.title: The landing zone as a governance foundation
02.imageBrief: The landing zone as a governance foundation — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: A landing zone establishes account, identity, logging and network baselines before teams deploy workloads.
Organizations supplies the hierarchy; Control Tower can orchestrate an opinionated baseline.
Separate security and workload accounts to reduce blast radius and centralize evidence.
02.decisionCue: Start with governance requirements and account boundaries before choosing workload services.

02.title: Organizations hierarchy: root, OUs and accounts
02.imageBrief: Organizations hierarchy: root, OUs and accounts — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: An account sits under one OU in the Organizations hierarchy and inherits applicable policies from the root and ancestor OUs.
SCPs set a maximum for member-account principals and do not grant IAM permissions.
The management account is not restricted by SCPs.
02.decisionCue: Use OUs for governance inheritance; assign workforce permissions to specific accounts.

02.title: Management account and delegated administrators
02.imageBrief: Management account and delegated administrators — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Keep organization-wide billing and governance tasks in the management account.
Register service-specific delegated administrator accounts to operate supported security services across member accounts.
Central log storage and audit access deserve distinct accounts and narrow roles.
02.decisionCue: Delegate service administration while keeping the management account lean.

02.title: Control Tower landing zone components
02.imageBrief: Control Tower landing zone components — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Control Tower builds on Organizations and orchestrates an opinionated landing zone with foundational accounts, access and controls.
Preventive, detective and proactive controls use different underlying mechanisms and have different scopes.
Account enrollment and drift monitoring do not replace application-team security work.
02.decisionCue: Choose Control Tower when standardized multi-account baselines and account vending are needed.

02.title: Account Factory and account lifecycle
02.imageBrief: Account Factory and account lifecycle — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Account Factory provisions or enrolls governed accounts and applies the landing-zone baseline.
OU selection changes inherited controls; IAM Identity Center assignments target specific accounts and permission sets.
The lifecycle includes approval, monitoring, drift review and careful retirement or migration.
02.decisionCue: Treat account provisioning as a governed product with a documented owner and lifecycle.

02.title: Preventive, detective and proactive controls
02.imageBrief: Preventive, detective and proactive controls — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Preventive controls prevent disallowed API changes; SCPs are one mechanism.
Proactive controls assess supported CloudFormation resources before provisioning.
Detective controls flag drift after deployment and require a remediation process.
02.decisionCue: Select the control type for the time you must detect or stop a violation.

02.title: SCPs: maximum permissions, not grants
02.imageBrief: SCPs: maximum permissions, not grants — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: SCPs define maximum permissions for principals in member accounts and never grant access.
An explicit Deny at any inherited level overrides an IAM Allow.
Allow-list designs need Allow at each hierarchy level; service-linked roles and management account have exceptions.
02.decisionCue: Use SCPs for organization-wide principal guardrails, not application permissions.

02.title: RCPs: guardrails around resources
02.imageBrief: RCPs: guardrails around resources — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: RCPs constrain supported resources in member accounts, including requests by external principals.
RCP support is service and action specific; S3, DynamoDB and SQS are examples.
RCPs never grant access and do not apply to management-account resources.
02.decisionCue: Use an RCP for resource-side data perimeter controls, especially where external callers are possible.

02.title: Policy inheritance and exception design
02.imageBrief: Policy inheritance and exception design — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Root and ancestor OU policies are inherited by member accounts.
A child OU or IAM Allow cannot override an applicable ancestor explicit Deny.
A necessary exception must be scoped at the policy that imposes the Deny, then tested and approved.
02.decisionCue: Design exceptions deliberately at the controlling policy layer.

02.title: Organization CloudTrail and immutable log archive
02.imageBrief: Organization CloudTrail and immutable log archive — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: An organization trail centralizes management events for current and future member accounts.
Configure data events selectively; S3 and Lambda data events are not universal by default.
Centralize delivery to a protected log archive and design S3/KMS permissions, retention and monitoring.
02.decisionCue: Treat CloudTrail as evidence and protect the log destination independently from workload accounts.

02.title: AWS Config aggregation across accounts
02.imageBrief: AWS Config aggregation across accounts — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Config recorders and rules operate in source accounts and Regions; aggregation centralizes their results.
A Config aggregator does not itself enable source recording or remediate resources.
Delivery to an S3 archive is a separate configuration history path.
02.decisionCue: Use an organization aggregator for cross-account visibility after recording is enabled.

02.title: GuardDuty and Security Hub organization view
02.imageBrief: GuardDuty and Security Hub organization view — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: GuardDuty detects potential threats from supported telemetry; Security Hub CSPM manages findings and enabled standards.
Delegated administrators and organization integration scale enrollment, but Region coverage needs configuration.
Findings need triage and response automation; neither service inherently remediates.
02.decisionCue: Connect detection to a central finding workflow and a separately authorized response.

02.title: Security Lake and security data pipelines
02.imageBrief: Security Lake and security data pipelines — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Security Lake normalizes supported security data to OCSF and stores it in regional S3 lakes.
Subscribers can query or access governed data according to their configured permissions.
It complements GuardDuty detection and Security Hub posture management.
02.decisionCue: Use Security Lake when centralized normalized evidence and subscriber analytics are needed.

02.title: CloudWatch Logs and AI invocation evidence
02.imageBrief: CloudWatch Logs and AI invocation evidence — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Application logs, Bedrock model invocation logs, and CloudTrail events serve different evidence needs.
Enable model invocation logging deliberately; CloudTrail does not automatically store prompt and response bodies.
Protect sensitive content with minimization, encryption, retention and scoped access.
02.decisionCue: Design observability and privacy controls together for AI workflows.

02.title: AWS RAM shares within and across the organization
02.imageBrief: AWS RAM shares within and across the organization — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: AWS RAM shares supported resources while the owning account keeps ownership and lifecycle control.
Organization/OU sharing and external account invitations have different setup and acceptance requirements.
Managed resource-share permissions and IAM principal permissions serve different roles; billing varies by service.
02.decisionCue: Choose RAM for supported shared infrastructure with documented owner and consumer duties.

02.title: Transit Gateway sharing and network ownership
02.imageBrief: Transit Gateway sharing and network ownership — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Share a Transit Gateway through RAM while retaining ownership in the network account.
Consumers create attachments; VPC and Transit Gateway route tables, DNS, security groups and NACLs still need deliberate configuration.
02.decisionCue: Use a shared network hub when central routing governance outweighs isolated VPC ownership.

02.title: Config rules and conformance packs
02.imageBrief: Config rules and conformance packs — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: AWS Config records supported resource configuration and evaluates rules; conformance packs group rules and optional remediation.
An aggregator gives centralized visibility but does not enable recording or fix noncompliance in source accounts.
02.decisionCue: Deploy recorder and rules in the target accounts before relying on an aggregator.

02.title: Security Hub CSPM controls and findings
02.imageBrief: Security Hub CSPM controls and findings — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Security Hub CSPM consolidates supported findings and evaluates security controls across configured accounts and Regions.
A finding is evidence, not a preventive block. Investigate and remediate in the owning account, then verify the control state.
02.decisionCue: Use posture controls for continuous assessment; pair with preventive policy where required.

02.title: Inspector scanning across accounts
02.imageBrief: Inspector scanning across accounts — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Amazon Inspector scans supported EC2, ECR and Lambda workloads for vulnerabilities under enabled coverage and delegated administration.
Prioritize findings, patch or rebuild the asset, and confirm a later scan. Inspector does not automatically apply patches.
02.decisionCue: Separate vulnerability discovery from remediation ownership.

02.title: Systems Manager Patch Manager at scale
02.imageBrief: Systems Manager Patch Manager at scale — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Systems Manager Patch Manager uses baselines, managed-node prerequisites, schedules and maintenance windows to patch fleets.
Roll out in waves, inspect compliance and failure reports, and resolve unreachable or unmanaged nodes separately.
02.decisionCue: A scheduled patch job alone does not prove fleet compliance.

02.title: Scenario: govern 100 accounts without blocking teams
02.imageBrief: Scenario: govern 100 accounts without blocking teams — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: For 100 accounts, provision accounts and guardrails centrally while assigning access to the intended accounts and roles.
Collect evidence centrally; maintain workload ownership for remediation and use scoped exceptions with review dates.
02.decisionCue: Scale the baseline without giving every team organization-wide access.

02.title: Governance architecture: final synthesis
02.imageBrief: Governance architecture: final synthesis — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Control Tower and Account Factory establish governed accounts; Organizations policies set permission ceilings.
RAM shares eligible infrastructure; CloudTrail, Config and Security Hub provide visibility; service teams remediate findings.
Document platform, security and workload ownership for each control.
02.decisionCue: Trace account foundation, preventive guardrails, evidence and response end to end.

02.title: Created, invited and moved accounts have different setup steps

03.title: Encryption decisions begin with data flow
03.imageBrief: Encryption decisions begin with data flow — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Trace data in transit, at rest, and in secrets stores; assign ownership and recovery requirements before choosing controls.
Certificate validation, service integration, key authorization and credential rotation are separate design decisions.
03.decisionCue: Inventory each data path and boundary.

03.title: KMS keys, envelopes and data keys
03.imageBrief: KMS keys, envelopes and data keys — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Envelope encryption uses a plaintext data key for bulk data and stores its encrypted copy with encrypted data.
KMS protects and decrypts the data key for authorized principals; protect plaintext key material in memory and discard it after use.
03.decisionCue: Distinguish key wrapping from bulk encryption.

03.title: AWS owned, AWS managed and customer managed keys
03.imageBrief: AWS owned, AWS managed and customer managed keys — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: AWS owned keys are abstracted from the customer; AWS managed keys are visible but AWS controls their policy and rotation.
Customer managed KMS keys give customer control over policy, grants and lifecycle; supported cross-account use needs a customer managed key.
03.decisionCue: Select the key type based on required control and integration.

03.title: Key policies, IAM policies and grants
03.imageBrief: Key policies, IAM policies and grants — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Every KMS key has one key policy; IAM allows require enabling delegation in the key policy or an appropriate direct key-policy grant.
KMS grants provide scoped permissions often used by services. Cross-account use requires authorization on the owning key and in the external principal account; explicit denies still apply.
03.decisionCue: Check both sides of cross-account authorization.

03.title: Automatic rotation and cryptoperiod choices
03.imageBrief: Automatic rotation and cryptoperiod choices — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: For eligible customer managed symmetric keys with AWS_KMS origin, automatic rotation changes key material while key ID, ARN and policy remain.
New encryptions use new material; KMS retains previous material for decryption. Rotation does not re-encrypt existing data.
03.decisionCue: Match rotation method and cryptoperiod to key type and origin.

03.title: Multi-Region keys and regional boundaries
03.imageBrief: Multi-Region keys and regional boundaries — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Related multi-Region keys share key ID and cryptographic material, allowing authorized cross-Region decryption of ciphertext.
Key policies, grants and aliases remain Regional and must be configured independently. Check each service integration before assuming it uses the multi-Region feature.
03.decisionCue: Choose replication for a real cross-Region cryptographic requirement.

03.title: S3 encryption and SSE-KMS trade-offs
03.imageBrief: S3 encryption and SSE-KMS trade-offs — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: SSE-S3 uses S3-managed encryption; SSE-KMS uses a KMS data key; DSSE-KMS applies a KMS data-key layer and a separate S3-managed layer.
A customer managed KMS key adds policy control and cross-account options. Plan KMS permissions, request load and costs; S3 Bucket Keys do not support DSSE-KMS.
03.decisionCue: Select by control and compliance need, then verify permissions.

03.title: EBS and RDS encryption lifecycle
03.imageBrief: EBS and RDS encryption lifecycle — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: EBS encryption is chosen for new volumes or encrypted snapshot copies; migrate existing unencrypted volumes through snapshot and new-volume workflows.
An existing unencrypted RDS DB cannot be encrypted in place. Copy its snapshot with encryption, restore a new DB and plan cutover.
03.decisionCue: Test restore and KMS access before the migration window.

03.title: Cross-account access to encrypted data
03.imageBrief: Cross-account access to encrypted data — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: A cross-account S3 read needs object authorization and KMS Decrypt authorization for the customer managed key.
Grant the external role in owner-account resource/key policies and allow required actions in the reader account; explicit denies and organization controls still apply.
03.decisionCue: Troubleshoot the S3 and KMS gates independently.

03.title: Secrets Manager rotation workflow
03.imageBrief: Secrets Manager rotation workflow — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Secrets Manager rotation creates a pending version, updates the target, tests it, then promotes it to current.
Rotation is configured for supported secret types and implementations. Applications must retrieve current credentials, tolerate transition and support rollback; never log plaintext.
03.decisionCue: Verify target update and application behavior, not only version labels.

03.title: Parameter Store versus Secrets Manager
03.imageBrief: Parameter Store versus Secrets Manager — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Parameter Store supports hierarchical configuration and KMS-encrypted SecureString, but does not itself rotate stored credentials automatically.
Secrets Manager is purpose-built for credentials, configured rotation and cross-Region replication. Choose on lifecycle and access needs, not encryption alone.
03.decisionCue: Use Secrets Manager when credential rotation is a requirement.

03.title: TLS 1.3 handshake and trust chain
03.imageBrief: TLS 1.3 handshake and trust chain — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: TLS 1.3 negotiates key shares and validates server identity through the certificate chain and hostname before the protected application session.
Trust anchors, validity, supported protocol/cipher policy and certificate deployment all affect success. A certificate does not itself encrypt bulk traffic.
03.decisionCue: Investigate certificate trust separately from protocol compatibility.

03.title: ACM public certificates for AWS endpoints
03.imageBrief: ACM public certificates for AWS endpoints — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: ACM public certificate issuance requires domain validation; attach the issued certificate to supported integrated endpoints.
CloudFront viewer certificates from ACM use us-east-1. ACM manages eligible renewals when validation and use conditions hold; imported certificate renewal is customer managed.
03.decisionCue: Check endpoint Region and renewal ownership.

03.title: AWS Private CA and private certificate lifecycle
03.imageBrief: AWS Private CA and private certificate lifecycle — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: AWS Private CA issues private certificates for internal trust domains; clients need the private CA chain in their trust stores.
Plan CA hierarchy, issuer permissions, renewal, revocation, monitoring and cost. Private certificates are not publicly trusted by default.
03.decisionCue: Choose private CA for managed internal PKI with explicit trust distribution.

03.title: End-to-end TLS through load balancers
03.imageBrief: End-to-end TLS through load balancers — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: An ALB HTTPS listener terminates client TLS. An HTTPS target group starts a separate TLS connection to the target; HTTP targets leave the backend leg unencrypted.
The target needs a certificate and compatible protocol configuration. Distinguish TLS re-encryption from TCP passthrough when reading an architecture scenario.
03.decisionCue: Draw both legs before claiming end-to-end encryption.

03.title: Mutual TLS for client authentication
03.imageBrief: Mutual TLS for client authentication — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: In ALB mutual TLS verify mode, the load balancer validates client certificates against its configured trust store and optional revocation list.
In ALB passthrough mode it forwards the client certificate chain in HTTP headers for application validation; this is not TCP TLS passthrough. Application authorization remains separate.
03.decisionCue: Select verification ownership before configuring mTLS.

03.title: Certificate renewal, revocation and expiry
03.imageBrief: Certificate renewal, revocation and expiry — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Diagnose hostname, chain trust, certificate validity and endpoint deployment separately.

ACM-issued eligible public certificates can renew under required validation/use conditions; imported certificates require customer replacement. Revocation checking depends on client and service behavior.
03.decisionCue: Monitor expiry and renewal evidence, not just issuance.

03.title: CloudHSM ownership and cluster operations
03.imageBrief: CloudHSM ownership and cluster operations — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: CloudHSM offers dedicated HSMs in a customer VPC; deploy HSMs across Availability Zones and integrate applications with supported client libraries.
AWS operates physical HSM infrastructure while the customer manages cluster, HSM users and keys. Encrypted backups and recovery planning remain essential.
03.decisionCue: Use dedicated HSM control only when requirement justifies operations.

03.title: CloudHSM versus KMS custom key store
03.imageBrief: CloudHSM versus KMS custom key store — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Direct CloudHSM application use requires HSM client integration and customer key/user operations.
A KMS CloudHSM custom key store retains KMS API and policy integration while storing non-extractable KMS key material in a customer-managed cluster; connection, quotas and health affect operations.
03.decisionCue: Compare API integration and operational responsibility.

03.title: External key store and control trade-offs
03.imageBrief: External key store and control trade-offs — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: An external key store sends authorized KMS cryptographic requests through a customer-operated XKS proxy to an external key manager.
External key material stays outside AWS; customer availability, latency, proxy security and recovery become dependencies. Check supported key/service scenarios before selecting XKS.
03.decisionCue: Choose XKS only for a firm external custody requirement.

03.title: Post-quantum threat model and migration inventory
03.imageBrief: Post-quantum threat model and migration inventory — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Inventory asymmetric key exchange, signatures, certificates, client lifetimes and long-lived sensitive data before migration.
Harvest-now-decrypt-later risk is most relevant to captured traffic that must remain confidential. Assess symmetric encryption separately from vulnerable asymmetric algorithms.
03.decisionCue: Prioritize long-lived secrets and hard-to-upgrade clients.

03.title: ML-KEM and hybrid key establishment
03.imageBrief: ML-KEM and hybrid key establishment — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: ML-KEM encapsulates a shared secret with a public key; its private key decapsulates the ciphertext. It is key establishment, not a signature or bulk encryption.
AWS KMS supports ML-KEM asymmetric keys and Encapsulate/Decapsulate. Hybrid post-quantum TLS for KMS API transport combines classical ECDH and ML-KEM; test client and network compatibility.
03.decisionCue: Separate KMS ML-KEM key operations from hybrid TLS transport.

03.title: ML-DSA signatures and verification
03.imageBrief: ML-DSA signatures and verification — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: ML-DSA signs with a protected private key and verifies with a public key for authenticity and integrity; it does not encrypt content.
Plan verifier compatibility, key specification and message-size handling. KMS ML-DSA supports RAW messages up to 4 KB and EXTERNAL_MU processing for larger messages.
03.decisionCue: Use ML-DSA for signatures, ML-KEM for shared secrets.

03.title: Crypto agility and staged rollout
03.imageBrief: Crypto agility and staged rollout — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: Pilot supported hybrid TLS clients and endpoints, then test proxies, middleboxes, handshake size, failure modes and telemetry before staged rollout.
Verify negotiated key exchange in evidence such as supported KMS CloudTrail tlsDetails for direct API calls. Migrate signatures with verifier compatibility and rollback planning.
03.decisionCue: Measure negotiated algorithms rather than assuming configuration succeeded.

03.title: Scenario: regulated multi-account encryption
03.imageBrief: Scenario: regulated multi-account encryption — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: In a regulated multi-account S3 design, the data account owns the bucket and customer managed KMS key. Producer and analyst access must be explicitly scoped.
A cross-account analyst read needs both S3 object and KMS Decrypt authorization. TLS protects transit; audit records usage but does not replace preventive permissions.
03.decisionCue: Check data permission, key permission and ownership separately.

03.title: Encryption architecture: final synthesis
03.imageBrief: Encryption architecture: final synthesis — an original, technically precise visual explanation grounded in the official SAP-C03 guide.
learningNotes: At rest: select service encryption, data-key design and KMS authorization. In transit: choose TLS policy and trusted certificates.
Key custody: weigh KMS, CloudHSM and XKS operations. Quantum readiness: inventory ML-KEM key establishment and ML-DSA signatures with staged compatibility testing.
03.decisionCue: Verify access, recovery and operational ownership at every boundary.

Supported public parameters and Secrets Manager references have different ownership and access behavior. Control recursive reads: GetParametersByPath can expose descendants of an authorized path. Review recursive access carefully; a broad parent-path permission can undermine a design that assumes child-path isolation. Authorize decrypted values: SecureString uses KMS and appropriate decrypt authorization. IAM access, KMS permissions, version selection and application caching all affect which configuration the application actually sees.

03.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Generate or reference a secret: A template can create a Secrets Manager secret and reference its value without embedding plaintext credentials in the template. Grant the deployment and consuming services only the required access. Separate deployment from rotation: Updating only the secret value does not automatically refresh a resource property containing a dynamic reference. CloudFormation resolves it during the relevant create/update operation. Keep consumers current: Configure an appropriate rotation workflow and consumer refresh strategy. 03.title: Cross-account secret reads must pass three authorization gates
03.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Caller identity permission: The consuming account's principal needs appropriate secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission for the intended secret ARN and context. Secret resource policy: The secret owner must grant the intended external principal access through a supported resource-based policy. Scope principals and conditions; avoid unintended external sharing. Customer-managed KMS key: For a secret encrypted with the owner's customer-managed key, permit the consumer's required decrypt use in applicable key/IAM policies. A secret permission alone does not authorize its encryption key.

03.title: KMS key material origin is different from key ownership
03.imageBrief: Module 09 style. AWS-generated or imported: A customer-managed key can use AWS-generated material or supported imported material. Imported-material expiry, deletion and reimport behavior require an explicit availability and recovery plan. CloudHSM custom key store: A supported custom key store backs KMS operations with a connected CloudHSM cluster. KMS integration remains, while cluster availability, capacity and operations become dependencies. External key store: An external key store delegates supported cryptographic operations to an external key manager through its proxy. This is different from importing material into KMS; latency and external outages affect AWS workloads.

03.title: CloudHSM TLS offload: keep the private key in the HSM
03.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Locate TLS termination: An ALB can terminate supported TLS with its configured certificate. A server-side TLS design instead terminates the connection at the application server; these are different key-placement choices. Use a supported HSM integration: For a supported web-server/cryptographic integration, an EC2 application invokes CloudHSM-backed private-key operations through the client/provider stack. CloudHSM does not become a transparent network proxy in the traffic path. Operate the dependency: Plan the HSM cluster, client configuration, private connectivity, certificate deployment and application recovery. HSM-backed keys do not remove TLS policy, trust-chain or availability responsibilities.

04.title: VPC boundary, CIDR and route-table mental model
04.imageBrief: VPC boundary, CIDR and route-table mental model — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: A VPC CIDR contains subnets in one Availability Zone each. Route tables choose a next hop for destination prefixes.
A route and matching security permissions are both needed for a viable traffic path.
04.decisionCue: Trace the address range, route, then security boundary.

04.title: Public and private subnet paths
04.imageBrief: Public and private subnet paths — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: Public, private and isolated subnet roles follow their effective routes. Direct IPv4 internet access also needs a public IPv4 address.
Private IPv4 outbound uses a NAT Gateway in a public subnet; an isolated database has no internet route.
04.decisionCue: Read the route table before classifying a subnet.

04.title: Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway and egress-only IGW
04.imageBrief: Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway and egress-only IGW — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: An IGW route and public IPv4 address enable direct public IPv4 access, subject to security controls.
NAT Gateway translates private IPv4 outbound; egress-only IGW allows initiated IPv6 outbound without translation.
04.decisionCue: Choose the exit by address family and inbound requirement.

04.title: Subnet sizing and address growth
04.imageBrief: Subnet sizing and address growth — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: AWS reserves five IPv4 addresses per subnet: first four and last. /24 yields 251 usable; /22 yields 1019.
Subnet CIDR size cannot change after creation; leave nonoverlapping space for AZ growth and ENIs.
04.decisionCue: Plan CIDRs for later growth, not only current hosts.

04.title: IPAM pools and allocation governance
04.imageBrief: IPAM pools and allocation governance — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: IPAM organizes address space into scopes and pools with governed allocation across accounts and Regions.
Monitor utilization and overlap; IPAM does not automatically renumber existing networks.
04.decisionCue: Centralize allocation before multi-account VPC growth.

04.title: Overlap detection and network renumbering
04.imageBrief: Overlap detection and network renumbering — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: Overlapping VPC CIDRs prevent unambiguous direct routing and VPC peering.
IPAM reveals conflicts; plan workload and DNS migration to nonoverlapping space. PrivateLink can expose a specific service without full network connectivity.
04.decisionCue: Identify overlap before interconnecting networks.

04.title: Route priority and longest-prefix match
04.imageBrief: Route priority and longest-prefix match — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: Longest-prefix match selects the most specific route in the associated subnet route table.
Check return routes and SG/NACL permissions after selecting a target.
04.decisionCue: Read the effective route table for the source subnet.

04.title: Security groups versus network ACLs
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose the enforcement boundary: Security groups attach to supported resources/ENIs and are stateful. Network ACLs apply at the subnet boundary and are stateless. A route and both applicable control layers must permit the intended path. Evaluate the rule model: Security groups use allow rules with implicit denial otherwise. Network ACLs support numbered allow/deny rules, evaluated in ascending order until a match; the first matching rule determines the result. Validate the return flow: Stateful security-group tracking normally permits response traffic for an allowed connection. NACLs need explicit return-direction rules, including the actual client ephemeral-port range; do not assume one OS's range fits every client.

04.title: VPC Flow Logs: what they show and miss
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose the observation scope: Create supported flow logging at VPC, subnet or ENI scope. Records summarize observed network flows and can be delivered to supported destinations such as CloudWatch Logs or S3. Read network evidence: Inspect interface, addresses, ports, protocol, byte/packet counts, time range, action and log status. Correlate forward and return directions; ACCEPT/REJECT alone does not identify every security or routing cause. Know the blind spots: Flow Logs are not packet captures, payload inspection or proof of application success. Some traffic is excluded, records may be delayed or skipped, and no flow record can also mean the packet never reached that observation point.

04.title: VPC endpoints: gateway versus interface
04.imageBrief: VPC endpoints: gateway versus interface — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.

Interface endpoints create managed ENIs with security groups and can support private DNS and hybrid access with routing/DNS.
04.decisionCue: Pick endpoint type by service, reachability and cost.

04.title: Private DNS for interface endpoints

This changes name resolution, not the application's IAM permissions. Prepare VPC and hybrid DNS: Check VPC DNS settings, private-zone conflicts and supported Resolver forwarding for other VPCs or on-premises clients. Creating an endpoint in one VPC does not automatically redirect every external client's DNS. Private addressing alone does not prove the intended access path or authorization.
