04.title: Endpoint policies and resource policies
04.imageBrief: Endpoint policies and resource policies — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: IAM identity permissions, endpoint policy, bucket/resource policy and applicable SCPs jointly determine access; explicit Deny prevails.
An endpoint policy filters but does not grant permissions alone; same-account identity permission need not require separate bucket-policy Allow.
04.decisionCue: Trace principal, action, resource and path.

04.title: VPC peering and nontransitive routes
04.imageBrief: VPC peering and nontransitive routes — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Peering connects two nonoverlapping VPCs directly, including across accounts/Regions.
It is nontransitive: A↔B and B↔C do not enable A↔C. Routes and security permissions are needed in both VPCs.
04.decisionCue: Use direct peerings sparingly; consider TGW for transit.

04.title: Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke attachments
04.imageBrief: Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke attachments — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: A regional Transit Gateway attaches VPCs and hybrid networks. A subnet route sends traffic to TGW; its associated TGW route table selects an attachment.
Reachability depends on association, propagation/static routes, destination return route and security controls.
04.decisionCue: Trace both directions through VPC and TGW routes.

04.title: Transit Gateway route tables and segmentation
04.imageBrief: Transit Gateway route tables and segmentation — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Each attachment consults its associated TGW route table for incoming traffic. Propagation or static routes populate selected destination paths.
Separate tables can allow Prod and Dev to reach shared services without allowing direct Prod↔Dev routing.
04.decisionCue: Validate forward and return paths for each segment.

04.title: Cross-account Transit Gateway sharing
04.imageBrief: Cross-account Transit Gateway sharing — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: A network account can share a regional TGW through AWS RAM with workload accounts, which create VPC attachments.
TGW owner controls route tables, associations and propagation; VPC routes and security controls remain separate.
04.decisionCue: Share the hub, then deliberately attach and route.

04.title: Cloud WAN core network and policy
04.imageBrief: Cloud WAN core network and policy — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Cloud WAN uses a global core network policy with regional edges, segments and attachment mapping.
Segment isolation and route sharing are policy decisions; do not assume automatic reachability.
04.decisionCue: Compare global policy needs with regional TGW hubs.

04.title: PrivateLink producer and consumer boundaries
04.imageBrief: PrivateLink producer and consumer boundaries — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: PrivateLink exposes a particular provider service through an interface endpoint without full VPC peering or CIDR routing.
Overlapping provider and consumer VPC CIDRs can work for service-level access.
04.decisionCue: Use for a specific private service across account boundaries.

04.title: PrivateLink endpoint service and NLB
04.imageBrief: PrivateLink endpoint service and NLB — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Provider associates an NLB with an endpoint service and manages allowed principals/acceptance.
Consumer creates interface endpoints in supported AZs and checks endpoint SG, DNS and service health.
04.decisionCue: Test both provider target health and consumer endpoint state.

04.title: PrivateLink versus peering versus Transit Gateway
04.imageBrief: PrivateLink versus peering versus Transit Gateway — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Peering provides direct nontransitive VPC routing; TGW centralizes many routed VPC/hybrid links; PrivateLink publishes a service only.
Choose according to needed reachability, overlap, security and cost.
04.decisionCue: Ask whether the consumer needs a network, routed hub or service.

04.title: VPC Lattice service-network connectivity
04.imageBrief: VPC Lattice service-network connectivity — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Lattice associates client VPCs and application services with a service network.
Listeners, target groups, optional IAM authorization and observability organize access across accounts.
04.decisionCue: Choose service networking for managed application access.

04.title: Lattice authentication, routing and observability
04.imageBrief: Lattice authentication, routing and observability — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: AWS_IAM auth uses signed requests and applicable service/service-network policies; NONE leaves Lattice authorization unenforced.
Rules and default actions select forwarding; inspect target health, access logs and metrics.
04.decisionCue: Trace authorization, routing and target health separately.

04.title: Centralized ingress and shared services VPC
04.imageBrief: Centralized ingress and shared services VPC — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: A central ingress ALB can use supported reachable private IP targets across connected VPCs.
Shared services and application VPCs need explicit routes, return paths and security controls; evaluate central failure domains.
04.decisionCue: Prove IP target health and return routing.

04.title: Centralized egress and NAT design
04.imageBrief: Centralized egress and NAT design — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: Spokes route through TGW to an egress VPC with public NAT Gateway and IGW.
Return routes, AZ alignment and TGW/NAT/cross-AZ cost need explicit design; NAT does not perform deep inspection.
04.decisionCue: Compare resilience and total traffic cost before centralizing.

04.title: Inspection VPC and symmetric routing
04.imageBrief: Inspection VPC and symmetric routing — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Stateful inspection requires forward and return traffic through the same flow-state endpoint.
Inspection VPC TGW appliance mode supports symmetry; native TGW-attached Network Firewall provides another managed option.
04.decisionCue: Validate route symmetry before changing firewall rules.

04.title: Gateway Load Balancer appliance insertion
04.imageBrief: Gateway Load Balancer appliance insertion — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: GWLB distributes flows to healthy third-party appliances with GENEVE encapsulation on UDP 6081.
GWLBe is the route target; inspection round trip returns through GWLB/GWLBe before VPC forwarding. Validate flow symmetry.
04.decisionCue: Separate steering from the appliance's inspection function.

04.title: AWS Network Firewall rule and endpoint path
04.imageBrief: AWS Network Firewall rule and endpoint path — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Network Firewall policy links stateless and stateful rule groups; stateless forward-to-stateful and stateful ordering/defaults affect evaluation.
Choose routed VPC endpoints/inspection VPC or native TGW network function attachment; the latter uses static routing and managed symmetry.
04.decisionCue: Validate placement, rule evaluation and flow/alert logs.

04.title: AWS WAF at application ingress
04.imageBrief: AWS WAF at application ingress — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: WAF inspects supported HTTP(S) requests using web ACL managed/custom/rate-based rules.
Allow/Block terminate, Count continues, and default action applies when no terminating action occurs. Tune with logs before enforcement.
04.decisionCue: Choose layer 7 protection and test false positives.

04.title: DDoS protection and edge placement
04.imageBrief: DDoS protection and edge placement — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Shield Standard provides baseline DDoS protection; Advanced adds capabilities for eligible protected resources under subscription.
Combine suitable edge services, origin restrictions, WAF, resilient applications, alarms and incident response.
04.decisionCue: Reduce origin exposure and validate operational readiness.

04.title: Layered segmentation and data perimeter
04.imageBrief: Layered segmentation and data perimeter — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Routing and SG/NACL/firewall controls apply to network boundaries; IAM/resource/endpoint policies authorize identities, resources and paths.
For S3, a bucket policy can require an approved endpoint. Test service-to-service access and supported condition keys.
04.decisionCue: Authorize identity, resource and trusted path.

04.title: IPv6 addressing and subnet allocation
04.imageBrief: IPv6 addressing and subnet allocation — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: Plan IPv6 allocation independently of IPv4; /56 to subnet /64 is an example, not a universal allocation requirement.
IPv6 needs addresses, supported services, routes and IPv6 security rules. Native IPv6 does not require NAT.
04.decisionCue: Plan prefixes and validate reachability separately.

04.title: Dual-stack rollout and DNS dependency
04.imageBrief: Dual-stack rollout and DNS dependency — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: Inventory IPv6 client, service, SDK and DNS dependencies before publishing AAAA records.
Test both address families end to end, verify supported load-balancer/target address modes, monitor and keep rollback.
04.decisionCue: A DNS record does not prove a functioning IPv6 path.

04.title: Egress-only internet gateway for IPv6
04.imageBrief: Egress-only internet gateway for IPv6 — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: An egress-only IGW supports initiated IPv6 internet connections and their responses, blocking unsolicited inbound.
Route ::/0 to the egress-only IGW and retain appropriate IPv6 SG/NACL rules; it performs no NAT.
04.decisionCue: Separate native IPv6 outbound control from IPv4 translation.

04.title: NAT64 and DNS64 for IPv6-only workloads
04.imageBrief: NAT64 and DNS64 for IPv6-only workloads — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: Subnet DNS64 synthesizes AAAA using 64:ff9b::/96 when only IPv4 A is available.
NAT Gateway NAT64 translates application traffic routed to that prefix; public NAT needs IGW for IPv4 internet. Resolver is not a traffic hop.
04.decisionCue: Verify DNS synthesis, translation route and application compatibility.

04.title: IPv6 security controls and logging
04.imageBrief: IPv6 security controls and logging — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: IPv4 rules do not cover IPv6. Audit IPv6 exposure, least privilege source ranges, routing and logs independently.
Support essential ICMPv6 such as path MTU discovery and validate security-stack/service support.
04.decisionCue: Test inbound and outbound in both address families.

04.title: Multi-Region network traffic patterns
04.imageBrief: Multi-Region network traffic patterns — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Route 53 DNS policies include latency, weighted, failover and location-based decisions; TTL/cache affects visibility.
Global Accelerator standard routing uses stable anycast entry addresses and healthy supported endpoints; regional application/data readiness remains essential.
04.decisionCue: Separate global client entry from private backend connectivity.

04.title: Cost-aware connectivity architecture
04.imageBrief: Cost-aware connectivity architecture — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Estimate hourly resources, processed GB, applicable AZ/Region/internet transfer and operational resilience along the actual path.
Compare endpoints, AZ-local NAT and centralized egress. TGW has no separate cross-AZ transfer charge between attachments; surrounding services can charge.
04.decisionCue: Apply current regional pricing to measured traffic volume.

04.title: Scenario: isolated multi-account application
04.imageBrief: Scenario: isolated multi-account application — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Separate TGW route-table association/propagation permits Prod and Dev to reach shared services without direct interconnection.
Use local S3 gateway endpoints and policies per VPC, approved inspected egress, nonoverlap and allowed/denied path tests.
04.decisionCue: Test the access matrix, including forbidden paths.

04.title: Scenario: inspect east-west and outbound traffic
04.imageBrief: Scenario: inspect east-west and outbound traffic — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Force east-west and outbound traffic through chosen inspection with deliberate routes and symmetric flow handling.
NAT translates IPv4; firewall enforces inspection. Validate logs, endpoint health, return direction, bypass prevention and AZ failure.
04.decisionCue: A direct working route can still violate inspection policy.

04.title: Network architecture decision synthesis
04.imageBrief: Network architecture decision synthesis — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Choose addressing, connectivity, internet access, security and resilience according to requirements and permitted traffic.
Prove identity, DNS, source route, inspection, destination and return path with logs, tests and cost analysis.
04.decisionCue: Explain the architecture choice and its failure/cost tradeoffs.

04.title: NAT instances: operate the forwarding host deliberately
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Configure the complete path: A NAT instance is an EC2 forwarding host in a suitable public subnet. Configure its public/EIP path, forwarding software and private-subnet route, and disable source/destination checking as required. Own the failure handling: Instance bandwidth, security configuration, patching, scaling and failover are your responsibility. A single forwarding host is a single failure domain. Compare managed egress: Use an appropriate managed NAT design when it meets the workload requirements. Do not infer that a legacy NAT-instance example supplies managed availability or automatic scaling.

04.title: Flow Logs: inspect the fields and the observation point
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. 05.title: DNS answers a name; routing carries the traffic
05.imageBrief: Separate DNS lookup from application connection; verify TTL, route and security independently.
learningNotes: DNS lookup returns an address; the application connects using separate routes, security and TLS.
TTL caches mean record changes need not be visible immediately.
05.decisionCue: Separate name resolution from application reachability.

05.title: Recursive resolution, authoritative answers and caching
05.imageBrief: Explain stub, recursive and authoritative roles, positive/negative caching and TTL.
learningNotes: Stub clients ask recursive resolvers, which use cache or authoritative DNS.
Positive and negative caching affect answers; changing a record does not flush existing caches.
05.decisionCue: Identify which cache and authority answered.

05.title: Public and private DNS views: split-horizon design
05.imageBrief: Compare public delegation with associated private zones and missing-record behavior.
learningNotes: Public and associated private hosted zones can give different answers for the same name.
A selected matching private zone does not automatically fall back to public DNS for missing names or types.
05.decisionCue: Inspect the client resolver and DNS view.

05.title: VPC DNS attributes, DHCP options and client resolvers
05.imageBrief: Distinguish DNS attributes and custom DNS forwarding; use inbound endpoints for remote resolution.
learningNotes: Inspect DHCP/custom resolver configuration and enableDnsSupport/enableDnsHostnames requirements for private DNS.
Remote clients should query Resolver inbound endpoints, not VPC base+2. Endpoint SGs differ from unfilterable AmazonProvidedDNS traffic.
05.decisionCue: Check client configuration and VPC attributes.

05.title: Private hosted zones and cross-account VPC association
05.imageBrief: Show association authorization, visibility, Profiles/RAM alternatives and routing independence.
learningNotes: Private-zone visibility comes from associations, including direct cross-account authorization/association or supported Profiles mechanisms.
VPC peering/TGW alone does not share the zone. Inbound endpoint VPC must resolve the intended private namespace.
05.decisionCue: Prove association and DNS visibility.

05.title: Namespace precedence, NXDOMAIN and reverse DNS
05.imageBrief: Most-specific zone/rule, same-domain forwarding precedence, no public fallback, PTR/reverse rules.
learningNotes: The most-specific matching private zone wins; same-domain forwarding rules take precedence over private hosted zones.
Missing names/types can yield NXDOMAIN/NODATA without public fallback. PTR uses reverse namespaces and may need supported auto-defined-rule overrides.
05.decisionCue: Check namespace specificity and precedence.

05.title: Inbound Resolver endpoints: on-premises queries into AWS
05.imageBrief: Forward from corporate DNS to resilient inbound endpoint IPs; associate relevant private zones.
learningNotes: Corporate DNS forwards AWS private suffixes to resilient inbound endpoint IPs over private connectivity.
Endpoint VPC zone visibility, DNS settings, UDP/TCP53, routes and response paths must all be correct.
05.decisionCue: Inbound queries enter AWS Resolver.

05.title: Outbound Resolver endpoints and conditional forwarding
05.imageBrief: Associate suffix-specific rules to client VPCs; route endpoint traffic to corporate DNS.
learningNotes: Associated suffix rules send AWS queries through an outbound endpoint to target corporate DNS IPs.
Most-specific rules and reverse namespaces matter; endpoint-to-target routes/security and return paths must work.
05.decisionCue: Outbound queries leave AWS Resolver toward corporate DNS.

05.title: Bidirectional hybrid DNS without forwarding loops
05.imageBrief: Separate namespace authority, forwarding and supported delegation; avoid looping catch-all rules.
learningNotes: Assign distinct AWS and corporate namespace authority and forward each suffix toward its owner.
Avoid sending the same suffix back and forth. Supported Resolver delegation modes differ from simple conditional forwarding.
05.decisionCue: Give each suffix one authoritative owner.

05.title: Resolver endpoint security, capacity and AZ resilience
05.imageBrief: UDP/TCP 53, stateful SG/stateless NACL response paths, multi-AZ IPs, capacity and health.
learningNotes: Inbound endpoint SG permits DNS from forwarders; outbound endpoint SG permits DNS to target servers. Stateful return is tracked.
NACL query/ephemeral response paths, TCP/UDP53, multi-AZ endpoint IPs, target redundancy and capacity monitoring are separate requirements.
05.decisionCue: Test both DNS transports and AZ failure.

05.title: Share Resolver rules across accounts with AWS RAM
05.imageBrief: Central rule ownership and consumer associations; connectivity and authorization remain distinct.
learningNotes: The network account can share forwarding rules using AWS RAM; workload VPCs associate them and use the owner endpoint.
Sharing does not grant private-zone visibility or app connectivity. Endpoint-to-target routes and security remain required.
05.decisionCue: Share policy with explicit consumer association.

05.title: Route 53 Profiles for consistent multi-VPC DNS
05.imageBrief: Bundle supported zone/rule/DNS Firewall associations and distribute with RAM; regional scope and precedence.
learningNotes: Regional Route 53 Profiles bundle supported private-zone associations, Resolver rules, DNS Firewall, logging and DNS settings for VPCs/accounts.
Local associations/settings can take precedence. PrivateLink interface VPC endpoint DNS integration is distinct from Resolver endpoints.
05.decisionCue: Verify effective configuration per VPC.

05.title: Resolve PrivateLink service names from hybrid networks
05.imageBrief: Private DNS, inbound endpoint forwarding, endpoint reachability and security; avoid application IP hardcoding.
learningNotes: Hybrid clients resolve configured service private DNS through an inbound endpoint, then connect separately to the interface endpoint private IP.
Check DNS view, VPN/DX routes, endpoint SG/service port and provider service state; avoid hardcoded ENI addresses.
05.decisionCue: Resolve privately, then validate the connection.

05.title: DNS Firewall: domain filtering and policy evaluation
05.imageBrief: Domain lists, priority/actions, alerts and failure behavior; DNS policy differs from packet inspection.
learningNotes: DNS Firewall evaluates lower numeric association/rule priorities first; ALLOW/BLOCK terminate matching evaluation while ALERT continues.
Default failure mode is closed. Query logs reveal decisions; DNS filtering does not replace egress controls or inspect all third-party encrypted DNS.
05.decisionCue: Use DNS filtering with network egress controls.

05.title: Resolver query logs and DNS observability
05.imageBrief: Query metadata, destinations, limits/cache effects, logging policy and troubleshooting correlation.
learningNotes: Regional Resolver query logging can send data to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose; confirm association and destination permissions.
Cached responses are not logged as new unique queries. Public-zone query logging is separate, and DNS logs are not packet capture.
05.decisionCue: Correlate logs with cache and client behavior.

05.title: Alias, CNAME, apex records and delegation
05.imageBrief: Use supported alias targets, CNAME constraints and public delegation; private delegation is separate.
learningNotes: Alias supports eligible AWS targets/same-zone records and zone-apex use subject to target/type constraints; CNAME maps to another DNS name and cannot be apex.
NS delegation changes authoritative ownership of a subdomain. Same-zone alias type must match its target record; ALB aliases use supported A/AAAA.
05.decisionCue: Choose record shape and authority separately.

05.title: DNS health checks and private application failover
05.imageBrief: Public checker reachability, CloudWatch-alarm health checks, alias target health and readiness limits.
learningNotes: Public Route 53 health checkers cannot directly probe private IPs; private failover can use metric/alarm-data-stream health checks or supported target health.
SetAlarmState does not force health-check state. Test readiness, missing data, all-unhealthy behavior, capacity and caching.
05.decisionCue: Use a reachable and meaningful health signal.

05.title: Route 53 routing policies, TTL and controlled shifts
05.imageBrief: Latency/weighted/failover/location policy decisions and health evaluation; cache affects visibility.
learningNotes: Choose simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity or multivalue according to the required decision and supported zone/record scope.
IP-based routing additionally uses configured client CIDR collections where supported. Weights affect DNS answers, not exact request percentages; TTL and health behavior matter.
05.decisionCue: Choose routing behavior, then account for caching.

05.title: Multi-Region private DNS and Resolver architecture
05.imageBrief: Regional endpoints/rules, zone associations and resilience; private backend connectivity and client entry.
learningNotes: A private hosted zone can associate VPCs across Regions; Resolver endpoints, rules, Profiles and hybrid paths are regional dependencies.
Deploy regional resilience explicitly, test cached answers and avoid unintended central-Region dependency.
05.decisionCue: Treat regional DNS paths as regional dependencies.

05.title: DNSSEC signing versus Resolver validation
05.imageBrief: Public-zone signing and chain of trust vs query validation; private scope limitations and SERVFAIL.
learningNotes: Public-zone signing and Resolver validation are distinct: KSK signs DNSKEY record set; ZSK signs zone record sets, with parent DS establishing trust.
DNSSEC authenticates/integrity-checks DNS, not encryption. Broken chains can cause SERVFAIL; monitor KMS/signing and plan safe rollover.
05.decisionCue: Validate the full DNSSEC chain of trust.

05.title: Troubleshoot timeout, NXDOMAIN, NODATA and SERVFAIL
05.imageBrief: Use caller/resolver/zone/rule/cache/log evidence; isolate security, DNSSEC and forwarding faults.
learningNotes: Use timeout, NXDOMAIN, NODATA and SERVFAIL as evidence with multiple possible causes.
Reproduce same caller/resolver/type; inspect effective zone/rule, cache, DNSSEC, firewall and upstream logs before changing routes.
05.decisionCue: Reproduce the exact caller, resolver and type.

05.title: Scenario: resilient multi-account hybrid DNS
05.imageBrief: Apply namespaces, zones, inbound/outbound rules, shared policy, logging, failure tests and cost tradeoffs.
learningNotes: Design distinct namespaces, regional inbound/outbound endpoints, private-zone/Profiles associations and shared suffix rules for each client view.
Validate DNS and app connectivity separately, including logs, policy, loop prevention, endpoint/AZ/Region failure and cost/retention.
05.decisionCue: Test both directions and every client view.

05.title: IP-based routing and geoproximity answer different questions
05.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Route by client CIDR: IP-based records use CIDR collections and location mappings for known client network ranges. Configure the supported unmatched-location behavior and consider DNS resolver/client-subnet visibility. Shift geographic catchments: Geoproximity uses resource/user location and a bias to expand or shrink the area served by an endpoint. It is different from country-based geolocation and measured-latency routing. Choose the control surface: Current geoproximity records can be configured directly where supported; Traffic Flow is useful for complex reusable policies. Do not repeat the older claim that every geoproximity configuration requires Traffic Flow.

05.title: Health checks: endpoint probes, aggregation and private signals
05.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Check a public endpoint: HTTP/HTTPS checks evaluate configured response criteria; TCP checks test connection behavior. Allow checker traffic, use the intended hostname/path, and validate optional response-string matching. Combine health evidence: Calculated checks combine child results using configured thresholds or logical rules. Checker aggregation and calculated-child limits are separate controls; consult current API/console limits. Monitor private readiness: Public health checkers cannot directly reach private endpoints. Use supported CloudWatch metric/alarm health signals and a prepared failover target; changing an alarm's display state is not a substitute for its metric data.

05.title: Traffic Flow and DNS caching make controlled changes repeatable
05.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Build reusable routing logic: Traffic Flow represents complex decision trees as versioned traffic policies and policy instances. A policy definition and the DNS records created from it are different resources. Test geographic and weighted decisions: Bias changes catchment size, while weights influence DNS-answer selection. Neither guarantees an exact share of individual HTTP requests because resolvers and clients cache answers. Plan rollout and rollback: Review TTL, record scope, health behavior, cost and the fallback for all-unhealthy or unmatched locations. Validate authoritative answers and client behavior before broad rollout.

05.decisionCue: Version the routing decision and test the cached client path, not just the policy editor.

06.title: Hybrid design starts with requirements
06.imageBrief: Hybrid design starts with requirements: Measure latency and jitter, steady and burst bandwidth, migration windows and critical backup capacity before selecting transport. Define encryption endpoints, acceptable interruption, operational effort and cost. Check shared devices, providers, circuits, power and sites.

Define encryption endpoints, acceptable interruption, operational effort and cost. Check shared devices, providers, circuits, power and sites.

06.title: VPN and Direct Connect: choose the transport
06.imageBrief: VPN and Direct Connect: choose the transport: VPN provides IPsec over a supported transport; Direct Connect provides a dedicated network path whose delivery must be provisioned. IPsec protects between VPN endpoints; application TLS can extend protection beyond them. Test backup throughput and convergence under representative load.
learningNotes: VPN provides IPsec over a supported transport; Direct Connect provides a dedicated network path whose delivery must be provisioned.
IPsec protects between VPN endpoints; application TLS can extend protection beyond them. Test backup throughput and convergence under representative load.
06.decisionCue: VPN provides IPsec over a supported transport; Direct Connect provides a dedicated network path whose delivery must be provisioned.

06.title: Two VPN tunnels, one customer-device risk
06.imageBrief: Two VPN tunnels, one customer-device risk: Each VPN connection has two AWS-side tunnels. Configure both; one customer appliance, ISP or site can still be a shared failure. Add a separate connection with independent equipment and dependencies. Measure route convergence and real application recovery separately.

Add a separate connection with independent equipment and dependencies. Measure route convergence and real application recovery separately.

06.title: VGW or Transit Gateway: choose the scope
06.imageBrief: VGW or Transit Gateway: choose the scope: A virtual private gateway attaches to one VPC and does not support VPN ECMP; Transit Gateway serves a broader routed network. Gateway selection does not replace subnet routes, return routes, segmentation, security groups or resilience testing.

Gateway selection does not replace subnet routes, return routes, segmentation, security groups or resilience testing.
06.decisionCue: A virtual private gateway attaches to one VPC and does not support VPN ECMP; Transit Gateway serves a broader routed network.

06.title: BGP, route propagation and return paths
06.imageBrief: BGP, route propagation and return paths: Static and dynamic BGP routing support depends on gateway type. Configure both AWS subnet routes and customer-side routes. TGW association selects the ingress attachment route table; propagation installs learned prefixes into selected tables. A learned route alone does not establish the entire return path.

06.decisionCue: Static and dynamic BGP routing support depends on gateway type. Configure both AWS subnet routes and customer-side routes.

06.title: VPN throughput, ECMP and acceleration
06.imageBrief: VPN throughput, ECMP and acceleration: Standard VPN tunnels support up to 1.25 Gbps; supported Large Bandwidth Tunnels support up to 5 Gbps per tunnel on Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN. Large Bandwidth Tunnels do not support acceleration. VPN ECMP requires dynamic routing; aggregate throughput does not give one flow the sum of all paths.

Large Bandwidth Tunnels do not support acceleration. VPN ECMP requires dynamic routing; aggregate throughput does not give one flow the sum of all paths.
06.decisionCue: Standard VPN tunnels support up to 1.25 Gbps; supported Large Bandwidth Tunnels support up to 5 Gbps per tunnel on Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN.

06.title: Direct Connect: physical link to BGP session
06.imageBrief: Direct Connect: physical link to BGP session
learningNotes: An AWS port dedicated to you; arrange carrier delivery and the facility cross-connect using the LOA-CFA.
A Direct Connect Partner provides a share of its connection. Accept it in your account.
50–500 Mbps options; 1, 2, 5, 10 or 25 Gbps. Availability varies by partner and location.
Customer router and last mile • facility cross-connect • AWS port • partner delivery, when hosted.
Commission separately: physical link • VLAN and VIF • BGP • application and return path.
06.decisionCue: Lead time is provider-dependent. A physical UP state is not proof of application access.

06.title: Private, public and transit virtual interfaces
06.imageBrief: Private, public and transit virtual interfaces: Public VIFs reach AWS public prefixes, not arbitrary internet destinations; comply with addressing and prefix ownership requirements. Private VIF/VGW and transit VIF/TGW designs use different gateway association models. BGP authentication does not encrypt application data.
learningNotes: Public VIFs reach AWS public prefixes, not arbitrary internet destinations; comply with addressing and prefix ownership requirements.
Private VIF/VGW and transit VIF/TGW designs use different gateway association models. BGP authentication does not encrypt application data.
06.decisionCue: Public VIFs reach AWS public prefixes, not arbitrary internet destinations; comply with addressing and prefix ownership requirements.

06.title: Direct Connect gateway: associations and allowed prefixes
06.imageBrief: Direct Connect gateway: associations and allowed prefixes: With VGW associations, allowed prefixes filter entire VPC CIDRs; a wider range does not synthesize an advertised summary. With TGW associations, configured allowed prefixes are originated from the Direct Connect gateway ASN. Avoid overlapping allowed prefixes across its TGW associations and validate actual downstream reachability.

With TGW associations, configured allowed prefixes are originated from the Direct Connect gateway ASN. Avoid overlapping allowed prefixes across its TGW associations and validate actual downstream reachability.
06.decisionCue: With VGW associations, allowed prefixes filter entire VPC CIDRs; a wider range does not synthesize an advertised summary.

06.title: Hybrid hub: Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway
06.imageBrief: Hybrid hub: Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway: The transit VIF provides transport and BGP; the Direct Connect gateway supplies associations and allowed advertisements; TGW route tables select downstream reachability. Configure VPC subnet routes and on-premises return routes. Shared connectivity does not mean every attachment should communicate; validate each Region independently.
learningNotes: The transit VIF provides transport and BGP; the Direct Connect gateway supplies associations and allowed advertisements; TGW route tables select downstream reachability.
Configure VPC subnet routes and on-premises return routes. Shared connectivity does not mean every attachment should communicate; validate each Region independently.
06.decisionCue: The transit VIF provides transport and BGP; the Direct Connect gateway supplies associations and allowed advertisements; TGW route tables select downstream reachability.

06.title: BGP policy: choose each direction
06.imageBrief: Two independent preferences
learningNotes: Your router controls traffic toward AWS; AWS selects paths toward your advertised networks.
For equal-length prefixes on private and transit VIFs, supported local-preference communities influence AWS path choice.
Use AS-path policy carefully; longest-prefix matching can override a less-specific backup.
Test both directions and failover; do not assume symmetry.
06.decisionCue: Two independent preferences

06.title: Direct Connect resilience: separate failure domains
06.imageBrief: Diversity is the design
learningNotes: Separate customer routers, power and access circuits.
Use independent AWS devices and multiple Direct Connect locations for location-failure protection.
A second circuit through the same provider conduit may share the same failure.
Test loss of a device, circuit and location; validate surviving capacity.
06.decisionCue: Diversity is the design

06.title: LAG: more capacity is not location diversity
06.imageBrief: One logical interface
learningNotes: Dedicated connections, same port speed, same Direct Connect endpoint. All members operate active/active.
The LAG goes down when live members fall below the configured threshold. Protect remaining links from overload.
Traffic is distributed across members. One flow is not guaranteed the sum of all link speeds.
06.decisionCue: LAG shares an endpoint failure domain. Use independent devices and locations for resilience.

06.title: Direct Connect backup: design the degraded mode
06.imageBrief: Failure is a workload event

Size backup throughput for critical workloads and defer noncritical transfers if needed.

06.title: Encryption: identify the protected boundary

learningNotes: TLS protects application sessions between their TLS endpoints.
IPsec protects routed traffic between VPN tunnel endpoints, including supported VPN-over-Direct-Connect designs.

06.title: Private IP VPN: encrypted overlay on private transport

06.title: Transit Gateway Connect: integrate SD-WAN
06.imageBrief: GRE carries traffic; BGP exchanges routes

Connect peers use GRE tunnels and BGP for appliance integration.

06.title: Hybrid operations: prove the complete path
06.imageBrief: Troubleshoot by layer
learningNotes: Check physical link, VIF, BGP session and prefix visibility before application policy.

06.title: Compute placement: put constraints first
06.imageBrief: Choose location before platform

Customer-managed on-premises compute gives local control with greater operational responsibility.

06.title: Outposts: local compute with regional ties
06.imageBrief: An extension with dependencies

06.title: Outposts racks: two networking roles
06.imageBrief: Service link and local gateway

06.title: Local Zones: nearby resources, regional dependencies
06.imageBrief: Lower latency needs a full path

06.title: EKS Anywhere: Kubernetes you operate
06.imageBrief: Local control plane, local responsibility

06.title: ECS Anywhere: external hosts, AWS orchestration

06.title: Disconnected operation: map every dependency
06.imageBrief: Local compute alone is insufficient

06.title: Hybrid case: justify the whole design
06.imageBrief: A decision checklist

06.title: VPN CloudHub: connect remote sites

06.title: Direct Connect SiteLink: site-to-site transport

07.title: Placement groups: locality, isolation and operational limits
07.imageBrief: Three rich conceptual hardware vignettes, cluster, rack spread and partition replicas. No exact rack topology. A short operation ribbon below. Cluster • performance Supported instances close together in one AZ for low latency and throughput. One rack is not guaranteed; the slower instance limits the pair. 09.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Authorize the signer: A presigned URL represents a particular signed request using the signer's permissions. Scope the operation, bucket/key and required request headers; possession of the URL can grant the intended bearer access. Bound the lifetime: The URL's expiry cannot outlive the usable signing credentials and may be constrained further by policy. Temporary role credentials can expire before a requested URL lifetime. Protect the workflow: Use HTTPS, controlled distribution and appropriate object/size/checksum conditions for the chosen upload mechanism. Test failures and avoid exposing long-lived credentials to the client.

10.title: EBS is persistent block storage within one AZ
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Attach inside the AZ: An EBS volume is a network block device. Attach it to a compatible EC2 instance in the same Availability Zone; most volumes have one attached instance. Multi-Attach is a specific io1/io2 exception. Reattach or restore: Detach safely and reattach within the same AZ. To move to another AZ, create a snapshot and restore a new volume in the target AZ; a volume itself does not span AZs. Plan persistence and performance: A volume can outlive its instance, depending on Delete on termination. Resize with supported Elastic Volumes operations, extend the OS filesystem, and check the instance EBS bandwidth.

10.title: EBS: choose the disk for the access pattern

Throughput-oriented HDD: st1 serves frequent sequential processing; sc1 serves colder throughput workloads. Both exclude boot-volume use.

10.title: gp2 and gp3 separate capacity from performance differently
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Capacity-linked gp2: Smaller gp2 volumes use a credit balance for bursts. Capacity, IOPS and throughput must be evaluated together. Independent gp3 controls: gp3 includes a baseline and permits additional IOPS and throughput within configuration constraints; capacity alone need not buy performance. Consistent io2 performance: Check I/O size, required latency and the complete instance-to-volume path; a published maximum is not an application guarantee.

10.title: Find the narrowest point in the EBS path
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Application demand: I/O size and queue depth change the relation between operations per second and transferred bytes. Volume limits: Inspect latency, queueing and throughput alongside provisioned IOPS. A large sequential read behaves differently from small random writes. Instance limits: Use suitable EBS-optimized instances and verify the instance bandwidth/IOPS ceiling before increasing the volume specification.

10.title: Snapshots capture changed blocks, not application intent
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Incremental blocks: The first snapshot includes written blocks; later snapshots capture changes. Deleting an earlier snapshot does not automatically invalidate later snapshots. Application consistency: Flush and quiesce appropriately before capture. Detachment is not mandatory; coordinate the database and all related volumes. Managed snapshot storage: Snapshots are EBS-managed recovery resources backed by S3; they are not ordinary objects in a customer-accessible snapshot bucket.

10.title: Restore in the target AZ and plan first-read latency

10.title: Automate recovery points with the right policy service
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Target with tags: DLM policies can target supported instances or volumes and create EBS snapshots or EBS-backed AMIs. Schedule and retain: Creation, retention, deletion and supported copy rules must match recovery and compliance requirements. 10.title: Encryption needs a working recovery key
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Regional default setting: Encryption by default applies prospectively to new volumes and snapshot copies in that account/Region. Existing data needs migration: Use an encrypted snapshot copy or encrypted new volume from a snapshot, then test and cut over. Enabling the setting does not alter old volumes. Authorize the recovery key: KMS policies and IAM permissions must permit the intended source, destination and recovery principals; cross-account keys need particular care.

10.title: Multi-Attach shares a block device, not a normal file share
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Shared block device: Each attached instance can read and write the same blocks. Multi-Attach is not an NFS/SMB server. Supported attachment scope: Up to 16 supported Nitro instances in one AZ; Linux supports io1/io2, Windows supports io2. Check current instance and driver requirements. Coordinate every writer: Use a cluster-aware filesystem or application and appropriate fencing. Mounting ordinary ext4/XFS concurrently can corrupt data.

10.title: Grow EBS deliberately; treat instance store as disposable
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Resize persistent storage: Supported size/type/performance changes are separate from extending the partition and filesystem in the guest OS. Migrate to shrink: EBS cannot shrink in place. Copy validated data to an appropriately smaller new volume, then perform a controlled cutover. Protect host-local data: Instance-store disks have instance-defined capacity and high local I/O. Use them for recreated scratch/cache; back up or replicate irreplaceable data.

10.title: EFS shares files across clients and AZs
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Managed shared NFS: NFSv4.1 and POSIX semantics suit Linux applications that require concurrent shared-file access; EFS is not native Windows SMB. Regional or One Zone: Regional storage spans AZs; One Zone accepts a single-AZ boundary. File capacity grows automatically, but network and performance planning remain. 10.title: A mount target is the network doorway to EFS
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Mount-target network path: Allow NFS TCP 2049 between the client and mount-target security groups; verify subnets, routes and return traffic. Keep the path local: Use an available mount target in the client AZ to avoid unnecessary cross-AZ paths. Mount-target availability differs for One Zone. Extend private connectivity: DX/VPN or supported VPC connectivity needs working DNS resolution or explicit target addressing. Provide redundant links and endpoints where required.

10.title: EFS authorization has several independent layers
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Network and IAM gates: Security groups provide reachability. Authenticated NFS mounts use the EFS helper and relevant IAM filesystem/client policies. POSIX file permissions: File UID/GID and directory read/write/execute permissions remain meaningful; IAM authorization does not replace POSIX checks. Access-point identity: Enforce an application root directory and identity. Restrict access-point use in policy; TLS protects transit and KMS protects stored data.

10.title: Choose EFS throughput to match demand
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose the performance mode: General Purpose is the recommended low-latency mode. Previous-generation Max I/O has higher operation latency and configuration restrictions. Match variable demand: Elastic throughput follows changing demand without requiring stored capacity to purchase throughput. Provision or use credits: Provisioned sets throughput separately from capacity. Bursting earns/spends credits based on Standard-class bytes; read metering differs from writes.

10.title: EFS lifecycle changes cost and access behavior
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose the access tier: Standard serves frequent file access; IA and Archive lower storage cost for less-used eligible files through lifecycle policies. Model the complete cost: Include retrieval/access costs, minimum durations, eligibility and latency. A lower storage rate does not guarantee a lower total bill. Respect the AZ boundary: Regional supports Archive; One Zone has a different class set. Automatic backups and restore readiness must fit the accepted failure boundary.

10.title: EFS replication is asynchronous recovery
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Asynchronous copy: Initial synchronization must finish before the destination data is available. Continued replication is asynchronous. Protected destination: The active destination is protected against application writes; prepare its mount targets, key access and policies before failover. Recover the application: Monitor TimeSinceLastSync and test a deliberate writable failover and client remount. Replication does not preserve an independent backup history.

10.title: Choose FSx by filesystem semantics
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Windows file semantics: Windows File Server: SMB and Active Directory. Parallel compute: Lustre: parallel compute and S3-linked datasets. ONTAP or OpenZFS: ONTAP: NFS, SMB and iSCSI; OpenZFS: managed NFS with ZFS capabilities.

10.title: Windows file shares keep Windows access controls
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Native Windows access: SMB with native NTFS semantics supports traditional enterprise shares, home directories and compatible Windows applications. Directory and permissions: Integrate Microsoft AD for authentication and use ACLs, quotas and DFS Namespaces to manage access and file organization. Compatible private clients: Linux needs a compatible SMB client. On-premises access needs private routing, DNS and AD connectivity over supported DX/VPN paths.

10.title: Multi-AZ Windows file storage protects the server tier
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Active and standby servers: Managed Multi-AZ deployments keep active and standby Windows file servers in different AZs. Reconnect after failover: Failover changes the serving node; applications must tolerate the interruption and reconnect through supported names. Keep recovery history: FSx-managed automatic daily backups are enabled by default. They preserve recovery history; Multi-AZ alone does not reverse a mistaken delete.

10.title: Change Windows file-system layout through migration
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Create the target layout: For a different AZ deployment or smaller allocated filesystem, provision a compatible new target. Copy and validate: Use a supported backup restore or DataSync migration. A backup restore is not a general way to shrink storage; migrate to a smaller target instead. Cut over deliberately: Stage the copy, pause writes, perform final synchronization, validate ACLs/data and switch application paths or DNS aliases.

10.title: Lustre feeds parallel compute
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Parallel shared files: Lustre provides concurrent shared-file access for HPC, ML, video processing, financial modeling and engineering workloads. Compute and storage together: Select storage media and throughput for metadata, small/random I/O or large/sequential I/O; benchmark the parallel workload. Link durable source data: Supported S3 repository linkage enables file processing without making S3 itself a general POSIX filesystem. Private hybrid clients still need supported connectivity.

10.title: Lustre durability depends on deployment and storage type
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Scratch is recreatable: Scratch does not replicate data or replace failed file servers. Keep inputs and valuable outputs independently recoverable. Persistent SSD and HDD: These persistent configurations replicate data within one AZ and replace failed file servers. Plan independent protection for an AZ failure. Persistent Intelligent-Tiering: Current Intelligent-Tiering replicates data across multiple AZs. Data durability and filesystem serving availability are different properties; test application recovery.

10.title: Lazy loading brings the working set to Lustre
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Import the namespace: Linked S3 metadata can be imported before all file content is present in Lustre. Load data on demand: Reads fetch the needed file data, allowing a job to start without downloading the complete repository; retained working data reduces repeated fetches. Export results explicitly: Configure automatic import/export or explicit repository tasks as supported. Changed output reaches S3 only through the configured export behavior.

10.title: ONTAP combines file and block protocols
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Serve file and block clients: Storage virtual machines and volumes expose NFS, SMB and iSCSI to compatible Linux, Windows, macOS and application clients. Protect and clone data: Snapshots, replication, efficient clones, compression and deduplication support migration and testing; changed data can consume additional space. Manage storage tiers: Manage SSD capacity, IOPS and capacity-pool tiering separately. Automatic tiering is not unlimited capacity or an unconditional automatic-shrink promise.

10.title: EBS walkthrough: modify, extend and verify
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Inspect the sandbox volume: Illustrative sandbox: inspect attachment, AZ, encryption, volume type and the instance EBS limits; take an appropriate recovery point. 10.title: EFS walkthrough: mount, authorize and prove sharing

10.title: Snapshot capture: protect the application's state
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Coordinate writes: A snapshot captures block storage, not an arbitrary database transaction. For stronger consistency, use a supported application-consistent procedure rather than assuming every attached snapshot is complete. 10.title: EFS access points: give each application its own view
10.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Enforce identity: Example: application A uses UID/GID 2101 through access point A. EFS can replace the client-supplied POSIX identity with the access-point identity. 10.title: EFS burst credits: connect storage size to throughput
